zone: Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish — Sawtooth Ridge, First Divide and Six Ridge
_areas_note: The grouping holds, but it is really THREE approaches sharing one trailhead rather than one. (1) Sawtooth Ridge — Cruiser, Lincoln, The Fin and The Horn are all Flapjack Lakes objectives, climbed from the lakes over Gladys Divide or Sawtooth Pass, and they are the only peaks here that behave as a cluster. (2) First Divide — Steel and Hopper are reached up the North Fork Skokomish valley to Home Sweet Home, about 13 miles in, a completely different trip that never goes near Flapjack. Mount Duckabush was CHECKED and KEPT: it stands at the head of the Duckabush valley beside Steel, and although its usual write-up describes the Marmot Lake and O'Neil Pass side, the shortest way to it is actually the Staircase side over First Divide and down to the Upper Duckabush junction, with the long Duckabush River trail from Brinnon serving the same ground from the east. (3) Mount Olson was also CHECKED and KEPT, but only just — it sits on Six Ridge, well west of everything else here, and it belongs to the Wynoochee group rather than the Sawtooth or Skokomish-Duckabush peaks. The Six Ridge trail does terminate on the North Fork Skokomish trail out of Staircase, so it is genuinely a Staircase objective, but it is at least as often done from the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead by way of Sundown Pass, which is a different road system entirely, and its camps share nothing with the Flapjack or First Divide camps. Treat it as an outlier in this zone, not a Sawtooth peak. THE WHOLE ZONE IS UNDER A FIRE CLOSURE. A large human-caused fire above Lake Cushman in July 2025 burned into the park and shut the area for a year. The developed Staircase area and its access road reopened in July 2026, but as of mid-August 2026 the wilderness trails beyond it were still closed — North Fork Skokomish to First Divide, Flapjack Lakes, Black and White Lakes, Gladys Divide, Home Sweet Home, Six Ridge, Four Stream and Wagonwheel Lake. Only the Staircase Rapids loop is open. Every site below is described as it functions normally; confirm the closure has lifted before planning any of it, and treat the eastern half of this zone as reachable only from the Duckabush side in the meantime.

sites.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
sites.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.
sites.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
sites.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
sites.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.

sites.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
sites.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.
sites.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
sites.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
sites.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.

sites.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
sites.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills
sites.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
sites.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
sites.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves NONE of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.

sites.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
sites.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet
sites.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
sites.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
sites.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.

sites.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
sites.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads
sites.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
sites.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
sites.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.

sites.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
sites.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through
sites.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
sites.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
sites.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.

sites.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
sites.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come
sites.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
sites.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
sites.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by fire, so at present it is the only way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.

sites.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
sites.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself
sites.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
sites.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
sites.notes: This entry exists for Mount Olson and for nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
